issues.legal_issue: A party who did not appeal a decree in a partition suit may receive relief in an appeal brought by another party.
material_facts: The trial court denied partition relief to some plaintiffs, who did not appeal that part of the decree.
The defendant appealed, and the High Court later granted relief to those plaintiffs in the second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The non-appealing plaintiffs were not barred from obtaining relief in the second appeal; the defendant’s objection was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: In a partition suit, the positions of plaintiffs and defendants are interchangeable, and a party may seek to be transposed while the suit is pending. Under Order 41 Rules 4 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court may reverse a decree in favour of non-appealing plaintiffs and make an order affecting defendants to do complete justice. The Court relied on Bhagwan Swaroop v. Mool Chand, Dr. P. Nalla Thampy Thera v. B.L. Shanker, and Chandramohan Ramchandra Patil v. Bapu Koyappa Patil.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding was a suit seeking partition and separate possession of property.
predicates.some_parties_appealed: One or more parties appealed the decree.
predicates.nonappealing_parties_claimed_partition_r: Other parties sought partition relief but did not themselves appeal the part of the decree denying it.

issues.definition: When a partition suit is appealed by some parties and other parties who did not appeal also claimed partition relief, the appellate court may grant relief to those non-appealing parties.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere in a second appeal with factual findings that are perverse because they disregard material evidence or rest on conjecture.
material_facts: The first appellate court reversed the trial court’s findings that a woman had married the deceased propositus and that her children were his children, although oral testimony and documentary records supported those findings.

The first appellate court also rejected the claim that a marriage-related deed was nominal and unacted upon, despite evidence of admissions in an earlier partition suit that it had been created to avoid a family member’s share and that the properties had not been handed over.

The High Court gave reasons based on the evidence for reversing the first appellate court’s findings, and the Supreme Court found that the first appellate court had overlooked material evidence and relied on conjecture and surmise.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court’s perverse approach raised a substantial question of law, and the High Court was justified in interfering with its findings in the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a substantial question of law may arise where factual findings are perverse. Findings may be perverse if they ignore or exclude relevant material, rely on irrelevant material, have no reliable evidentiary support, or rest on conjecture and surmise; a High Court may not, however, routinely substitute its own view for factual findings. The Court relied on Municipal Committee, Hoshiarpur v. Punjab State Electricity Board, including its discussion of Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh, Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Anjuman-E-Ismail Madris-Un-Niswan, Dinesh Kumar v. Yusuf Ali, and Bharatha Matha v. R. Vijaya Renganathan; Illoth Valappil Ambunhi v. Kunhambu Karanavan; and K.N. Nagarajappa v. H. Narasimha Reddy, which discussed Narayan Sitaramji Badwaik v. Bisaram.

rule.if: second_appeal and first_appellate_court_reversed_trial_findings and material_evidence_was_overlooked and findings_rest_on_conjecture

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court was a second appeal.
predicates.first_appellate_court_reversed_trial_fin: The first appellate court reversed factual findings made by the trial court.
predicates.material_evidence_was_overlooked: The first appellate court failed to take account of material oral or documentary evidence bearing on the disputed facts.
predicates.findings_rest_on_conjecture: The first appellate court’s findings rested on conjecture or surmise rather than a proper appreciation of the evidence.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when the first appellate court reverses trial findings after overlooking material evidence and its findings rest on conjecture, the High Court may interfere with those perverse findings.
